test_text.title: The meaning and power of smell

article.title: The meaning and power of smell

items.sentence_raw: The sense of smell, or olfaction, is powerful.
Odours affect us on a physical, psychological and social level.
For the most part, however, we breathe in the aromas which surround us without being consciously aware of their importance to us.
It is only when the faculty of smell is impaired for some reason that we begin to realise the essential role the sense of smell plays in our sense of well-being.
items.explain: Q33: The introduction says *'It is only when the faculty of smell is impaired for some reason that we begin to realise the essential role'*. **'Impaired'** means **'damaged'**. So we become aware of its importance when our ability to smell is damaged. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: A survey conducted by Anthony Synott at Montreal's Concordia University asked participants to comment on how important smell was to them in their lives.
It became apparent that smell can evoke strong emotional responses.
items.explain: Q27: Paragraph A says smell *'can evoke strong emotional responses'* and that our perception of smell includes *'the experiences and emotions associated with them'*. **'Emotional responses'** and **'feelings'** are the same idea. So the heading is **viii** — the relationship between smell and feelings.

items.sentence_raw: A scent associated with a good experience can bring a rush of joy, while a foul odour or one associated with a bad memory may make us grimace with disgust.
Respondents to the survey noted that many of their olfactory likes and dislikes were based on emotional associations.

Such associations can be powerful enough so that odours that we would generally label unpleasant become agreeable, and those that we would generally consider fragrant become disagreeable for particular individuals.
The perception of smell, therefore, consists not only of the sensation of the odours themselves, but of the experiences and emotions associated with them.
items.explain: Q27: Paragraph A says smell *'can evoke strong emotional responses'* and that our perception of smell includes *'the experiences and emotions associated with them'*. **'Emotional responses'** and **'feelings'** are the same idea. So the heading is **viii** — the relationship between smell and feelings.

items.sentence_raw: Odours are also essential cues in social bonding.
items.explain: Q28: Paragraph B starts by saying odours are *'essential cues in social bonding'*. It gives examples like infants recognising their mothers and adults identifying spouses by scent. **'Social bonding'** means **'personal relationships'**. So the heading is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: One respondent to the survey believed that there is no true emotional bonding without touching and smelling a loved one.
In fact, infants recognise the odours of their mothers soon after birth and adults can often identify their children or spouses by scent.
items.explain: Q28: Paragraph B starts by saying odours are *'essential cues in social bonding'*. It gives examples like infants recognising their mothers and adults identifying spouses by scent. **'Social bonding'** means **'personal relationships'**. So the heading is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: In one well-known test, women and men were able to distinguish by smell alone clothing worn by their marriage partners from similar clothing worn by other people.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says people could *'distinguish by smell alone clothing worn by their marriage partners'*. The question asks what belonging to husbands and wives they can recognise — the answer is **clothing**.

items.sentence_raw: Most of the subjects would probably never have given much thought to odour as a cue for identifying family members before being involved in the test, but as the experiment revealed, even when not consciously considered, smells register.
items.explain: Q34: The experiment showed that people could identify their partner's clothing by smell, but the passage adds that most subjects *'would probably never have given much thought to odour as a cue'* before the test. This means we use smell without realising it. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: In spite of its importance to our emotional and sensory lives, smell is probably the most undervalued sense in many cultures.
items.explain: Q29: Paragraph C says smell is *'probably the most undervalued sense in many cultures'*. **'Undervalued'** means **'not appreciated'**. The whole paragraph explains why people think our sense of smell is weak. So the heading is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: The reason often given for the low regard in which smell is held is that, in comparison with its importance among animals, the human sense of smell is feeble and undeveloped.
items.explain: Q35: Paragraph C first gives a common belief: that the human sense of smell is *'feeble and undeveloped'*. Then the writer says *'While it is true... they are still remarkably acute'*, which means this common belief is wrong. The writer is **rejecting a common belief**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: While it is true that the olfactory powers of humans are nothing like as fine as those possessed by certain animals, they are still remarkably acute.
items.explain: Q35: Paragraph C first gives a common belief: that the human sense of smell is *'feeble and undeveloped'*. Then the writer says *'While it is true... they are still remarkably acute'*, which means this common belief is wrong. The writer is **rejecting a common belief**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Our noses are able to recognise thousands of smells, and to perceive odours which are present only in extremely small quantities.
Smell, however, is a highly elusive phenomenon.
Odours, unlike colours, for instance, cannot be named in many languages because the specific vocabulary simply doesn't exist.
items.explain:
Q30: Paragraph D explains that odours *'cannot be named in many languages because the specific vocabulary simply doesn't exist'*. We have to say *'It smells like...'* and struggle to describe it. This is exactly about **'the difficulties of talking about smells'**. So the heading is **i**.

Q38: The passage says odours cannot be named in many languages because *'the specific vocabulary simply doesn't exist'*. The question says they lack the appropriate something — that something is **vocabulary**.

items.sentence_raw: 'It smells like...,' we have to say when describing an odour, struggling to express our olfactory experience.
items.explain: Q30: Paragraph D explains that odours *'cannot be named in many languages because the specific vocabulary simply doesn't exist'*. We have to say *'It smells like...'* and struggle to describe it. This is exactly about **'the difficulties of talking about smells'**. So the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: Nor can odours be recorded: there is no effective way to either capture or store them over time.
In the realm of olfaction, we must make do with descriptions and recollections.
This has implications for olfactory research.
Most of the research on smell undertaken to date has been of a physical scientific nature.
Significant advances have been made in the understanding of the biological and chemical nature of olfaction, but many fundamental questions have yet to be answered.
Researchers have still to decide whether smell is one sense or two - one responding to odours proper and the other registering odourless chemicals in the air.
items.explain:
Q36: Paragraph E says researchers *'have still to decide whether smell is one sense or two'*. This means even the basic definition of smell is not yet decided. **'Have still to decide'** means it is **yet to be defined**. So the answer is **D**.

Q39: The passage mentions smell may respond to *'odourless chemicals in the air'*. **'Odourless'** means they do not smell. So the answer is **chemicals**.

items.sentence_raw: Other unanswered questions are whether the nose is the only part of the body affected by odours, and how smells can be measured objectively given the nonphysical components.
Questions like these mean that interest in the psychology of smell is inevitably set to play an increasingly important role for researchers.
items.explain: Q31: Paragraph E says many questions remain unanswered, and that *'interest in the psychology of smell is inevitably set to play an increasingly important role for researchers'*. This points to what will happen in the future. So the heading is **iii** — future studies into smell.

items.sentence_raw: However, smell is not simply a biological and psychological phenomenon.
Smell is cultural, hence it is a social and historical phenomenon.
Odours are invested with cultural values: smells that are considered to be offensive in some cultures may be perfectly acceptable in others.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says smells considered offensive *'in some cultures may be perfectly acceptable in others'*. The question asks where odours are regarded as unpleasant or not — the answer is **cultures**.

items.sentence_raw: Therefore, our sense of smell is a means of, and model for, interacting with the world.
Different smells can provide us with intimate and emotionally charged experiences and the value that we attach to these experiences is interiorised by the members of society in a deeply personal way.
Importantly, our commonly held feelings about smells can help distinguish us from other cultures.
items.explain: Q32: Paragraph F says our feelings about smells *'can help distinguish us from other cultures'*. **'Distinguish us from other cultures'** means smells help define which group we belong to. So the heading is **v** — the interpretation of smells as a factor in defining groups.

items.sentence_raw: The study of the cultural history of smell is, therefore, in a very real sense, an investigation into the essence of human culture.
